items.title: How to debate, from a two-time world champion
items.description:
Two-time debate champion Bo Seo breaks down why arguments fail: the four bad-faith personas that hijack conversations, a four-question framework for picking fights worth having, and the surprising Cold War standoff between Nixon and Khrushchev that gives us a model for staying cool under pressure.  
 
 This video  How to debate, from a two-time world champion  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Can we be certain that time really exists?
items.description: From both a philosophical and a scientific perspective, we’re taught to doubt, question, and be skeptical of everything. Even the reality of ourselves and our own experiences cannot be taken for granted, as we must make certain assumptions about how trustworthy our measurement sensors — and our own senses, for that matter — actually are in order to arrive at any satisfactory conclusions. items.title: The secret your brain uses to decide how much pain you feel
items.description:
We treat pain like a plumbing problem. Something in the body is broken, so we block the signal with medication or cut it out with surgery. The opioid epidemic is what happens when that is the only model we have.

items.title: History shows that human progress is a myth
items.description:
There are two different kinds of stories. 
 The first is the linear story. The characters start at position A and end at position B, having beaten all the baddies, and married the right person. The real story is about the transformation that happens along the way. This is a story about direction. Mostly, it’s about progress. We move from naïve to wise, raw to cooked, NPC to hero.

items.title: Does the expanding Universe stretch space or create new space?
items.description: It’s been nearly a full century, almost 100 years, since humanity first reached a revolutionary conclusion about the nature of our Universe: space itself cannot and does not remain static, but rather evolves with the passage of time. items.title: NASA image shows Earth’s lumpiness — exaggerated 10,000 times
items.description:
No, the Earth is not flat. But it’s not exactly  round  either. Nor is it — let us stop you right there, smartypants — an oblate spheroid. 
 Close enough, but not a geoid 
 An oblate spheroid is a geometrically smooth model of our planet that, due to its rotation, bulges at the equator and flattens at the poles. While it is close enough to be used by GPS systems, for instance, it’s not  quite  right: It doesn’t account for the lumpiness of our actual Earth.
